claim: About 243 million people are infected with schistosomiasis worldwide.
source: About 243 million people are infected with schistosomiasis worldwide, of whom ~ 93% reside in sub-Saharan Africa where children carry the greatest burden of the disease.
evidence: This is a factual statement about global schistosomiasis prevalence, but no specific citation or data source is provided in the text for this number.

claim: Approximately 93% of people infected with schistosomiasis worldwide reside in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: About 243 million people are infected with schistosomiasis worldwide, of whom ~ 93% reside in sub-Saharan Africa where children carry the greatest burden of the disease.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the geographical distribution of schistosomiasis.

claim: Children carry the greatest burden of schistosomiasis disease in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: About 243 million people are infected with schistosomiasis worldwide, of whom ~ 93% reside in sub-Saharan Africa where children carry the greatest burden of the disease.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the demographic distribution of disease burden.

claim: Schistosomiasis accounted for 1.43 million disability-adjusted life-years lost in 2017.
source: In the tropics and subtropics, schistosomiasis is a major cause of disability among neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) accounting for 1.43 million disability-adjusted life-years lost in 2017 (GBD 2017 Disease and Injury Incidence and Prevalence Collaborators, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the GBD 2017 study.

claim: Schistosomiasis is a major cause of disability among neglected tropical diseases in the tropics and subtropics.
source: In the tropics and subtropics, schistosomiasis is a major cause of disability among neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) accounting for 1.43 million disability-adjusted life-years lost in 2017 (GBD 2017 Disease and Injury Incidence and Prevalence Collaborators, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and the quantitative data on DALYs.

claim: Infection with schistosomiasis occurs when trematodes of the genus Schistosoma shed by infected freshwater snails penetrate the skin upon contact with infested water.
source: Infection occurs when trematodes of the genus Schistosoma shed by infected freshwater snails (an intermediate host) penetrate the skin upon contact with infested water (Colley et al., 2014).
evidence: This mechanism of infection is supported by a citation to Colley et al., 2014.

claim: Freshwater snails serve as an intermediate host for Schistosoma trematodes.
source: Infection occurs when trematodes of the genus Schistosoma shed by infected freshwater snails (an intermediate host) penetrate the skin upon contact with infested water (Colley et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated explicitly and supported by citation.

claim: Intensity of schistosomiasis infection in the human host is a function of the parasite load.
source: Intensity of infection in the human host is a function of the parasite load and can indirectly be quantified by the number of eggs excreted.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about infection intensity measurement.

claim: Intensity of schistosomiasis infection can indirectly be quantified by the number of eggs excreted.
source: Intensity of infection in the human host is a function of the parasite load and can indirectly be quantified by the number of eggs excreted.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about diagnostic methods.

claim: Host variations in worm burden have been attributed to recent chemoprophylaxis, heterogeneities in exposure and host susceptibility.
source: Host variations in worm burden has been attributed to recent chemoprophylaxis, heterogeneities in exposure and host susceptibility (Colley et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Colley et al., 2014.

claim: Most human schistosomiasis infections in sub-Saharan Africa are due to Schistosoma mansoni and Schistosoma haematobium.
source: Most human infections in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) are due to Schistosoma mansoni, which causes intestinal schistosomiasis and Schistosoma haematobium responsible for urogenital schistosomiasis (Lai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lai et al., 2015.

claim: Schistosoma mansoni causes intestinal schistosomiasis.
source: Most human infections in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) are due to Schistosoma mansoni, which causes intestinal schistosomiasis and Schistosoma haematobium responsible for urogenital schistosomiasis (Lai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated explicitly and supported by citation.

claim: Schistosoma haematobium is responsible for urogenital schistosomiasis.
source: Most human infections in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) are due to Schistosoma mansoni, which causes intestinal schistosomiasis and Schistosoma haematobium responsible for urogenital schistosomiasis (Lai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated explicitly and supported by citation.

claim: Schistosoma haematobium has the widest geographical coverage in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: However, Schistosoma haematobium has the widest geographical coverage in SSA and is the main cause of infection in the Hlabisa sub-district, where our study is based (Saathoff et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Saathoff et al., 2004.

claim: Schistosoma haematobium is the main cause of schistosomiasis infection in the Hlabisa sub-district.
source: However, Schistosoma haematobium has the widest geographical coverage in SSA and is the main cause of infection in the Hlabisa sub-district, where our study is based (Saathoff et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Saathoff et al., 2004.

claim: A measure of piped water access by individuals/households is less sensitive than a measure of piped water coverage at the community level for assessing impact on Schistosoma haematobium infection.
source: We argued that a measure of piped water access by individuals/households, which is commonly used in the existing literature (Grimes et al., 2014), is less sensitive than a measure of piped water coverage at the community level.
evidence: This is the authors' argument based on their hypothesis and is supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: Higher community coverage of piped water reduces an individual's exposure to parasitic agents (direct benefit).
source: Our hypothesis is that a higher community coverage of piped water reduces both an individual's exposure to parasitic agents (direct benefit) as well as the number of contacts that infectious individuals in the surrounding have with open water bodies, thus decreasing the overall transmission intensity of Schistosoma haematobium within the community (indirect benefit).
evidence: This is stated as the authors' hypothesis.

claim: Higher community coverage of piped water decreases the number of contacts that infectious individuals have with open water bodies.
source: Our hypothesis is that a higher community coverage of piped water reduces both an individual's exposure to parasitic agents (direct benefit) as well as the number of contacts that infectious individuals in the surrounding have with open water bodies, thus decreasing the overall transmission intensity of Schistosoma haematobium within the community (indirect benefit).
evidence: This is stated as the authors' hypothesis.

claim: Higher community coverage of piped water decreases the overall transmission intensity of Schistosoma haematobium within the community (indirect benefit).
source: Our hypothesis is that a higher community coverage of piped water reduces both an individual's exposure to parasitic agents (direct benefit) as well as the number of contacts that infectious individuals in the surrounding have with open water bodies, thus decreasing the overall transmission intensity of Schistosoma haematobium within the community (indirect benefit).
evidence: This is stated as the authors' hypothesis.

claim: Every percentage increase in community piped water (in the prior 7 years) was associated with a 2.5% decrease in the odds of Schistosoma haematobium infection in the baseline survey.
source: In this baseline parasitological survey, we showed that every percentage increase in community piped water (in the prior 7 years) was associated with a 2.5% decrease in the odds of Schistosoma haematobium infection.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous baseline analysis.

claim: The baseline parasitological survey did not determine if community piped water coverage reduced re-infection rates among children treated with praziquantel.
source: However, we did not determine if community piped water coverage reduced re-infection rates among the same children who were treated with praziquantel during the baseline survey.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the previous baseline study.

claim: Two consecutive rounds of follow-up of infected children were undertaken between September and December of 2007 (round 1), and between April and August of 2008 (round 2).
source: Here, we report the results of two consecutive rounds of follow-up of infected children, which were undertaken between September and December of 2007 (round 1), and between April and August of 2008 (round 2) respectively.
evidence: This describes the study design and timing.

claim: This is the first study to systematically evaluate the impact of community piped water coverage on Schistosoma haematobium re-infection rates following treatment with praziquantel.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to systematically evaluate the impact of community piped water coverage on Schistosoma haematobium re-infection rates following treatment with praziquantel and therefore address a major public health evidence gap highlighted in a recent review (Grimes et al., 2015).
evidence: This is the authors' claim about the novelty of their study, supported by citation to a review identifying the evidence gap.

claim: A major public health evidence gap regarding the impact of community piped water coverage on Schistosoma haematobium re-infection rates was highlighted in a recent review.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to systematically evaluate the impact of community piped water coverage on Schistosoma haematobium re-infection rates following treatment with praziquantel and therefore address a major public health evidence gap highlighted in a recent review (Grimes et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grimes et al., 2015.

claim: A total of 2105 children from all 33 primary schools in the study area consented to participate in the baseline parasitological survey.
source: During the baseline parasitological survey, a total of 2105 children from all 33 primary schools located in a contiguous geographical area in rural KwaZulu-Natal consented to participate in the study.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study sample size.

claim: Of the 2105 children who consented to participate, 1976 were residents in the study area.
source: Of these participants, 1976 were residents in the study area (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The prevalence of baseline Schistosoma haematobium infection was 16.9% (95%CI: 15.2–18.6).
source: The prevalence of baseline infection was 16.9% (95%CI: 15.2–18.6) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a measured prevalence with confidence intervals from the baseline survey.

claim: Out of 333 microscopically confirmed infections at baseline, 253 (76%) consented to screening for Schistosoma haematobium re-infection at round 1.
source: Out of the 333 microscopically confirmed infections at baseline, 253 (76%) consented to screening for Schistosoma haematobium re-infection at round 1 and 125 consented for screening at round 2 (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a factual statement about cohort retention.

claim: 125 children consented for screening at round 2.
source: Out of the 333 microscopically confirmed infections at baseline, 253 (76%) consented to screening for Schistosoma haematobium re-infection at round 1 and 125 consented for screening at round 2 (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a factual statement about cohort retention.

claim: The prevalence of light re-infection at round 1 was 15.4% (95%CI: 11.2–20.5).
source: The prevalence of light re-infection and heavy re-infection was 15.4% (95%CI: 11.2–20.5) and 8.7% (95%CI: 5.5–12.9) for round 1, and 12.8% (95%CI: 7.5–20.0) and 6.4% (95%CI: 2.8–12.2) for round 2, respectively.
evidence: This is a measured prevalence with confidence intervals.

claim: The prevalence of heavy re-infection at round 1 was 8.7% (95%CI: 5.5–12.9).
source: The prevalence of light re-infection and heavy re-infection was 15.4% (95%CI: 11.2–20.5) and 8.7% (95%CI: 5.5–12.9) for round 1, and 12.8% (95%CI: 7.5–20.0) and 6.4% (95%CI: 2.8–12.2) for round 2, respectively.
evidence: This is a measured prevalence with confidence intervals.

claim: The prevalence of light re-infection at round 2 was 12.8% (95%CI: 7.5–20.0).
source: The prevalence of light re-infection and heavy re-infection was 15.4% (95%CI: 11.2–20.5) and 8.7% (95%CI: 5.5–12.9) for round 1, and 12.8% (95%CI: 7.5–20.0) and 6.4% (95%CI: 2.8–12.2) for round 2, respectively.
evidence: This is a measured prevalence with confidence intervals.

claim: The prevalence of heavy re-infection at round 2 was 6.4% (95%CI: 2.8–12.2).
source: The prevalence of light re-infection and heavy re-infection was 15.4% (95%CI: 11.2–20.5) and 8.7% (95%CI: 5.5–12.9) for round 1, and 12.8% (95%CI: 7.5–20.0) and 6.4% (95%CI: 2.8–12.2) for round 2, respectively.
evidence: This is a measured prevalence with confidence intervals.

claim: The geometric mean egg count at round 1 was 16.7 (95%CI: 9.4–29.6) eggs/10 mL.
source: The geometric mean egg counts were 16.7 (95%CI: 9.4–29.6) eggs/10 mL for round 1 and 18.2 (95%CI: 6.5–50.6) eggs/10 mL for round 2.
evidence: This is a measured value with confidence intervals.

claim: The geometric mean egg count at round 2 was 18.2 (95%CI: 6.5–50.6) eggs/10 mL.
source: The geometric mean egg counts were 16.7 (95%CI: 9.4–29.6) eggs/10 mL for round 1 and 18.2 (95%CI: 6.5–50.6) eggs/10 mL for round 2.
evidence: This is a measured value with confidence intervals.

claim: In the pooled analysis (n = 378), 119 (31.5%) were girls.
source: In the pooled analysis (n = 378), 119 (31.5%) were girls and 69 (18.3%) were below 11 years of age.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the pooled analysis.

claim: In the pooled analysis (n = 378), 69 (18.3%) were below 11 years of age.
source: In the pooled analysis (n = 378), 119 (31.5%) were girls and 69 (18.3%) were below 11 years of age.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the pooled analysis.

claim: The overall rate of re-infection was 36 (95%CI: 27–48) infections/100 person-years of follow-up.
source: Overall the rate of re-infection was 36 (95%CI: 27–48) infections/100 person-years of follow-up.
evidence: This is a calculated rate with confidence intervals.

claim: The median community piped water coverage in 2007 was 91.2% (inter quartile range (IQR), 71.0–97.7).
source: The median community piped water coverage in 2007 was 91.2% (inter quartile range (IQR), 71.0–97.7) (Figure 2B) and was geographical heterogeneous (Tanser et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a measured value with IQR, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Community piped water coverage in 2007 was geographically heterogeneous.
source: The median community piped water coverage in 2007 was 91.2% (inter quartile range (IQR), 71.0–97.7) (Figure 2B) and was geographical heterogeneous (Tanser et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The proportion of children with heavy infection at baseline increased from 5.1% (95%CI: 1.9–10.7) among children ≤ 9 years old to 14.8% (95%CI: 10.3–20.4) among children ≥ 14 years of age.
source: As we previously noted, the proportion of children with heavy infection at baseline increased from 5.1% (95%CI: 1.9–10.7) among children ≤ 9 years old to 14.8% (95%CI: 10.3–20.4) among children ≥ 14 years of age (χ2-test-of-trend=22.96, p<0.001) (Tanser et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the baseline analysis with statistical test results.

claim: The increase in proportion of children with heavy infection at baseline with age was statistically significant (χ2-test-of-trend=22.96, p<0.001).
source: As we previously noted, the proportion of children with heavy infection at baseline increased from 5.1% (95%CI: 1.9–10.7) among children ≤ 9 years old to 14.8% (95%CI: 10.3–20.4) among children ≥ 14 years of age (χ2-test-of-trend=22.96, p<0.001) (Tanser et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statistical test result from the baseline analysis.

claim: In the re-infection cohort, the proportion of heavy re-infection decreased from 13.0% (95%CI: 6.1–23.3) among children < 11 years of age to 6.9% (95%CI: 2.8–13.8) among children > 12 years of age.
source: In contrast, in the re-infection cohort, the proportion of heavy re-infection decreased with increasing age, from 13.0% (95%CI: 6.1–23.3) among children < 11 years of age to 6.9% (95%CI: 2.8–13.8) among children > 12 years of age (χ2-test-of-trend=3.317, p=0.3454) although with lower statistical power.
evidence: This is a measured proportion with confidence intervals from the re-infection cohort.

claim: The decrease in proportion of heavy re-infection with age was not statistically significant (χ2-test-of-trend=3.317, p=0.3454).
source: In contrast, in the re-infection cohort, the proportion of heavy re-infection decreased with increasing age, from 13.0% (95%CI: 6.1–23.3) among children < 11 years of age to 6.9% (95%CI: 2.8–13.8) among children > 12 years of age (χ2-test-of-trend=3.317, p=0.3454) although with lower statistical power.
evidence: This is a statistical test result.

claim: The decline in re-infection prevalence towards older children was more marked in girls than boys.
source: The decline in re-infection prevalence towards older children was more marked in girls than boys (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Every percentage point increase in community piped water coverage was associated with 4.4% decline in mean re-infection intensity (IRR = 0.96, 95% CI: 0.93–0.98, p=0.004).
source: In the pooled adjusted negative binomial model (n = 378), a percentage point increase in community piped water coverage in the area surrounding a child's residence was associated with 4.4% decline in mean re-infection intensity (Model 2 in Table 2; incidence rate ratio (IRR) = 0.96, 95% CI: 0.93–0.98, p=0.004).
evidence: This is a result from the negative binomial regression model with statistical significance.

claim: Lower piped water coverage areas were associated with significantly higher mean egg counts.
source: Lower piped water coverage areas were associated with significantly higher mean egg counts albeit with relatively low numbers of children living at low piped water coverages (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Every percentage increase in community piped water coverage was associated with approximately 3% decrease in intensity of re-infection at follow-up round 1.
source: An analysis of each follow-up survey round separately (N = 253 and N = 125 for round 1 and round 2 respectively) revealed a consistent pattern in which community piped water was strongly protective against Schistosoma haematobium re-infection intensity. That is, every percentage increase in community piped water coverage was associated with ~3% and~8% decrease in intensity of re-infection at follow-up round 1 and 2 respectively (Model 2 of Supplementary file 1 and Model 2 of Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from the separate analysis of round 1.

claim: Every percentage increase in community piped water coverage was associated with approximately 8% decrease in intensity of re-infection at follow-up round 2.
source: An analysis of each follow-up survey round separately (N = 253 and N = 125 for round 1 and round 2 respectively) revealed a consistent pattern in which community piped water was strongly protective against Schistosoma haematobium re-infection intensity. That is, every percentage increase in community piped water coverage was associated with ~3% and~8% decrease in intensity of re-infection at follow-up round 1 and 2 respectively (Model 2 of Supplementary file 1 and Model 2 of Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from the separate analysis of round 2.

claim: Boys were at a higher risk of intense re-infection than girls in both follow-up rounds.
source: In both follow-up rounds, boys were at a higher risk of intense re-infection than girls (Model 2 of Supplementary file 1, and Model 2 of Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from the regression models in both rounds.

claim: Dropout was higher among participants residing away from water bodies (>2 km) in follow-up round 1.
source: Dropout was higher among participants residing away from water bodies (>2 km) in follow-up round 1 and among girls in follow-up round 2.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about cohort retention patterns.

claim: Dropout was higher among girls in follow-up round 2.
source: Dropout was higher among participants residing away from water bodies (>2 km) in follow-up round 1 and among girls in follow-up round 2.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about cohort retention patterns.

claim: There was no clear pattern between dropout and piped water coverage.
source: However, there was no clear pattern between dropout and piped water coverage.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about cohort retention patterns.

claim: One significant cluster of higher than average geometric mean egg count (radius = 6.93 km, geometric mean egg count = 54.95, p=0.006) was detected near the Mfolozi river in the southeastern part of the study area.
source: In addition, we detected one significant cluster of higher than average geometric mean egg count (radius = 6.93 km, geometric mean egg count = 54.95, p=0.006) near the Mfolozi river in the southeastern part of the study area.
evidence: This is a result from spatial scan statistics shown in Figure 5.

claim: The detected cluster of high re-infection intensity partially overlapped with one of the existing clusters detected in the baseline analysis.
source: This cluster partially overlapped with one of the existing clusters detected in our baseline analysis (Tanser et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citation to the baseline analysis.

claim: The scaleup of piped water coverage in the local community surrounding a child's residence is strongly protective against Schistosoma haematobium infection and re-infection after treatment.
source: Taking these findings together with our previously reported baseline analyses (Tanser et al., 2018), we conclude that the scaleup of piped water coverage in the local community surrounding a child's residence is strongly protective against Schistosoma haematobium infection and re-infection after treatment.
evidence: This is the authors' conclusion based on their current and previous findings.

claim: There is a strong positive relationship between age and Schistosoma haematobium infection prevalence.
source: Unsurprisingly, we previously (Tanser et al., 2018) noted a strong positive relationship between age and Schistosoma haematobium infection prevalence likely due to the increasing cumulative exposure to infested water (and hence infection with Schistosoma haematobium) with increasing age (Dawaki et al., 2016; Wami et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The positive relationship between age and Schistosoma haematobium infection prevalence is likely due to increasing cumulative exposure to infested water with increasing age.
source: Unsurprisingly, we previously (Tanser et al., 2018) noted a strong positive relationship between age and Schistosoma haematobium infection prevalence likely due to the increasing cumulative exposure to infested water (and hence infection with Schistosoma haematobium) with increasing age (Dawaki et al., 2016; Wami et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations.

claim: Younger age groups have a higher risk of re-infection with Schistosoma haematobium.
source: In this study and consistent with previous work (Mbanefo et al., 2014; Roberts et al., 1993), we observed a higher risk of re-infection among the younger age groups where intensity of exposure to contaminated water is likely higher (Mbanefo et al., 2014; Chandiwana et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated as a finding consistent with previous work, supported by citations.

claim: Intensity of exposure to contaminated water is likely higher among younger age groups.
source: In this study and consistent with previous work (Mbanefo et al., 2014; Roberts et al., 1993), we observed a higher risk of re-infection among the younger age groups where intensity of exposure to contaminated water is likely higher (Mbanefo et al., 2014; Chandiwana et al., 1991).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations.

claim: Naturally acquired immunity against Schistosoma haematobium infection reduces both intensity of infection and infection prevalence in older age groups in endemic areas.
source: Evidence has shown that naturally acquired immunity against Schistosoma haematobium infection reduces both intensity of infection and infection prevalence in older age groups in endemic areas (Mitchell et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mitchell et al., 2011.

claim: Treatment with praziquantel enhances host protective immunity by exposing large quantities of the parasite antigens required to develop immunity.
source: Whilst developing this protective immunity take time, treatment with praziquantel has been shown to enhance host protective immunity by exposing large quantities of the parasite antigens required to develop immunity (Roberts et al., 1993; Chisango et al., 2019; Fukushige et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Naturally acquired immunity may have played a role in the observed decline in prevalence of re-infection with increasing age following treatment, but the impact is likely minimal given the narrow age range examined.
source: In this study, naturally acquired immunity may also have played a role in the observed decline in prevalence of re-infection with increasing age following treatment. However, the impact is likely to be minimal given the narrow age range that was examined.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: Differences in gender roles resulting from cultural differences may differentially predispose girls or boys to increased contact with infested water.
source: Differences in gender roles resulting from cultural differences may differentially predispose girls (Gyuse et al., 2010) or boys (Chandiwana et al., 1991; Liao et al., 2011; Geleta et al., 2015; Senghor et al., 2015) to increased contact with infested water therefore increasing their risk of re-infection with Schistosoma haematobium after treatment (Mbanefo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Gender differences in contact with infested water explain the heterogeneous findings on gender observed across different geographical settings.
source: These differences explain the heterogeneous findings on gender observed across different geographical settings (Mbanefo et al., 2014; Liao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations.

claim: Girls were at a lower risk of intense re-infection compared to boys in this study.
source: In our study and consistent with studies conducted elsewhere (Chandiwana et al., 1991; Liao et al., 2011; Geleta et al., 2015; Senghor et al., 2015), girls were at a lower risk of intense re-infection compared to boys (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated as a finding consistent with other studies, supported by citations and shown in Table 2.

claim: Exposure to Schistosoma haematobium infested water in the study area is heterogeneous.
source: We detected a significant local cluster of intense re-infection in the current analysis that partially overlaps with the cluster of Schistosoma haematobium infection observed in the baseline survey (Tanser et al., 2018), demonstrating that exposure to Schistosoma haematobium infested water in the study area is heterogeneous and that transmission is concentrated in certain key locations in keeping with evidence from this and other settings (Brooker, 2007; Simoonga et al., 2008; Manyangadze et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by citations.

claim: Schistosoma haematobium transmission is concentrated in certain key locations.
source: We detected a significant local cluster of intense re-infection in the current analysis that partially overlaps with the cluster of Schistosoma haematobium infection observed in the baseline survey (Tanser et al., 2018), demonstrating that exposure to Schistosoma haematobium infested water in the study area is heterogeneous and that transmission is concentrated in certain key locations in keeping with evidence from this and other settings (Brooker, 2007; Simoonga et al., 2008; Manyangadze et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by citations.

claim: Schistosoma haematobium clusters can potentially be targeted with available control interventions to interrupt transmission.
source: Schistosoma haematobium clusters can potentially be targeted with available control interventions to interrupt transmission (Simoonga et al., 2008) and subsequently achieve elimination (Bergquist et al., 2017; Ross et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a recommendation supported by citations.

claim: Targeting Schistosoma haematobium clusters with control interventions can subsequently achieve elimination.
source: Schistosoma haematobium clusters can potentially be targeted with available control interventions to interrupt transmission (Simoonga et al., 2008) and subsequently achieve elimination (Bergquist et al., 2017; Ross et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a recommendation supported by citations.

claim: The study utilized a cohort of children who were treated for Schistosoma haematobium infection at baseline and had two consecutive rounds of follow-up to assess re-infection intensity.
source: Our study had important strengths: firstly, we utilized a cohort of children who were treated for Schistosoma haematobium infection at baseline and had two consecutive rounds of followed-up to assess re-infection intensity.
evidence: This describes the study design.

claim: The study design presents a strong basis to directly quantify the causal association between community piped water coverage and Schistosoma haematobium infection.
source: This design presents a strong basis to directly quantify the causal association between community piped water coverage and Schistosoma haematobium infection.
evidence: This is the authors' assessment of their study design.

claim: The study was nested within a large population-based cohort in rural KwaZulu-Natal province with detailed homestead level geospatial data.
source: Secondly, the study was nested within a large population-based cohort in rural KwaZulu-Natal province with detailed homestead level geospatial data linking each child to their residence within the demographic surveillance area.
evidence: This describes the study setting and data availability.

claim: The study had access to a comprehensive survey of household level piped water use and asset ownership conducted in 2007.
source: Thirdly, we had access to a comprehensive survey of household level piped water use and asset ownership conducted in 2007 that we utilized to derive an index of community piped water coverage and household wealth index.
evidence: This describes the data sources used in the study.

claim: The study utilized longitudinal databases of environmental predictors of disease infection to adjust for potential confounding in the regression models.
source: Finally, we utilized longitudinal databases of environmental predictors of disease infection, described in detail in our previous work (Tanser et al., 2018), to adjust for potential confounding in the regression models.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach and data sources.

claim: The study did not assess praziquantel treatment effect after drug administration.
source: A limitation to our study is that we did not assess praziquantel treatment effect after drug administration.
evidence: This is stated as a study limitation.

claim: It may be difficult to ascertain whether a positive diagnosis was due to re-infection or treatment failure without assessing treatment effect.
source: It may therefore be difficult to ascertain whether a positive diagnosis was due to re-infection or treatment failure.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the study limitation.

claim: Approximately 80% cure rates at 4 weeks after treatment with praziquantel have been reported in KwaZulu-Natal.
source: However, approximately 80% cure rates at 4 weeks after treatment with praziquantel has been reported in KwaZulu-Natal (Saathoff et al., 2004) and Côte d'Ivoire (N'Goran et al., 2001), suggesting that most positive diagnoses after treatment were likely re-infections.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Saathoff et al., 2004.

claim: Approximately 80% cure rates at 4 weeks after treatment with praziquantel have been reported in Côte d'Ivoire.

claim: Sex was a strong independent predictor of infection with Schistosoma haematobium in the baseline analysis.

claim: The impact of community piped water coverage on Schistosoma haematobium infection was greater among girls than among boys in the baseline analysis.

claim: A higher proportion of attrition among girls will potentially bias the association of piped water on re-infection intensity towards the null hypothesis.

claim: The current global MDA coverage for schistosomiasis is approximately 20%.
source: Although this strategy has clear short-term benefits of reduced morbidity, sustained benefits are uncertain given the current global MDA coverage of circa 20%, low drug compliance and efficacy, and rapid re-infection rates (Ross et al., 2017).

claim: Improved access to piped water in the community significantly reduces the intensity of re-infection among school going children.

claim: Schistosoma haematobium control programs should consider scaleup of piped water coverage in the community as a preventive strategy against re-infection to supplement the MDA strategy.

source: Schistosoma haematobium infection status was determined using the urine reagent strips for evaluating microhematuria with confirmation using microscopy diagnosis.

claim: A single oral dose of 40 mg/kg body weight of praziquantel was administered to children with detectable microhematuria.
source: A single oral dose of 40 mg/kg body weight of praziquantel was administered to children with detectable microhematuria following recommended World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines on Schistosoma haematobium preventive chemotherapy (Saathoff et al., 2004; WHO Expert Committee on the Control of Schistosomiasis, 2002) under strict supervision of trained nurses.
evidence: This describes the treatment protocol.

claim: Praziquantel was administered following recommended WHO guidelines on Schistosoma haematobium preventive chemotherapy.
source: A single oral dose of 40 mg/kg body weight of praziquantel was administered to children with detectable microhematuria following recommended World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines on Schistosoma haematobium preventive chemotherapy (Saathoff et al., 2004; WHO Expert Committee on the Control of Schistosomiasis, 2002) under strict supervision of trained nurses.

claim: Praziquantel was administered under strict supervision of trained nurses.
source: A single oral dose of 40 mg/kg body weight of praziquantel was administered to children with detectable microhematuria following recommended World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines on Schistosoma haematobium preventive chemotherapy (Saathoff et al., 2004; WHO Expert Committee on the Control of Schistosomiasis, 2002) under strict supervision of trained nurses.
evidence: This describes the treatment administration procedure.

claim: Children who had false negative urine reagent strip results were subsequently traced back in school and became eligible for treatment and inclusion in the cohort analysis.
source: Children who had false negative urine reagent strip results (based on microscopy gold standard) were subsequently traced back in school, and became eligible for treatment and inclusion in the cohort analysis.

source: However, because of the time lag between laboratory testing and treatment, some children with a false negative test results missed treatment for baseline infection if they were absent from school during tracing and were therefore not eligible for inclusion in the cohort analysis.
evidence: This describes a limitation in the follow-up procedure.

claim: Urine samples were collected between 10:00 and 12:00 hr using 500 mL honey jars.
source: Urine samples were collected between 10:00 and 12:00 hr using 500 mL honey jars (one sample per child).
evidence: This describes the sample collection procedure.

claim: Each sample testing for infection was done in two stages: testing using urinalysis reagent strips in schools and confirmatory microscopy analysis in the laboratory.
source: Each sample testing for infection was done in two stages: 1) testing using urinalysis reagent strips (Bayer Uristix) in schools and 2) confirmatory microscopy analysis in the laboratory.
evidence: This describes the diagnostic procedure.

claim: Urine samples were aliquoted and processed in duplicates of 10 mL sub-samples and diluted using 2% methiolate in 5% Formalin.
source: The urine samples were aliquoted and processed in duplicates of 10 mL sub-samples and diluted using 2% methiolate in 5% Formalin.
evidence: This describes the laboratory processing procedure.

claim: Filtration was done using polycarbonate filters with diameter of 25 mm and 8.0 μm pore size.
source: Filtration was done using the polycarbonate filters (diameter of 25 mm and 8.0 μm pore size).
evidence: This describes the filtration methodology.

claim: Eggs were counted by trained laboratory technicians and expressed per 10 mL of urine.
source: Eggs were counted by trained laboratory technicians and expressed per 10 mL of urine.
evidence: This describes the egg counting procedure.

claim: The primary outcome of interest was the subject level egg count determined by averaging the duplicate egg counts for each participating child in each follow-up round.
source: The primary outcome of interest was the subject level egg count determined by averaging the duplicate egg counts for each participating child in each follow-up round.
evidence: This describes the primary outcome measure.

claim: Egg counts were categorized into heavy (≥50 eggs/10 mL) and light (<50 eggs/10 mL) re-infections following WHO classification guidelines.
source: We categorized egg counts into a priori groups of heavy (≥50 eggs/10 mL) and light (<50 eggs/10 mL) re-infections following WHO classification guidelines (WHO Expert Committee on the Control of Schistosomiasis, 2002) on intensity of re-infection with Schistosoma haematobium.
evidence: This describes the categorization method based on WHO guidelines.

claim: A re-infection date was randomly imputed between the treatment date and the testing date assuming a uniform distribution for all children who were re-infected.
source: Given that the exact date of re-infection after treatment is not observed, we randomly imputed a re-infection date between the treatment date and the testing date assuming a uniform distribution (Vandormael et al., 2018) for all children who were re-infected with Schistosoma haematobium in both rounds of follow-up.
evidence: This describes the statistical method for handling interval-censored data.

claim: Community piped water coverage for each residential homestead was derived from a weighted two-dimensional Gaussian kernel of 2 km radius using data from the 2007 homestead level survey.
source: We derived the community piped water coverage for each residential homestead of the participating child from a weighted two-dimensional Gaussian kernel of 2 km radius using data from the 2007 homestead level survey on access to piped water (Figure 6B).
evidence: This describes the method for deriving the exposure variable.

claim: The 2 km radius for the Gaussian kernel was selected based on a tradeoff between sensitivity to local variations and robustness to random noise.
source: The 2 km radius was selected based on our previous analysis in which a tradeoff between sensitivity to local variations and robustness to random noise was considered (Tanser et al., 2018).
evidence: This explains the rationale for the kernel radius selection, supported by citation.

claim: The negative binomial model was the best fit to the data among the plausible count models examined.
source: The negative binomial model was the best fit to our data among the plausible count models that we examined in a data driven model selection procedure (Tang et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the model selection process.

claim: Univariable analyses retained significant covariates at p<0.1.
source: We used univariable analyses (retaining significant covariates at p<0.1) and backwards exclusion of non-significant covariates (p>0.05) to arrive at a final parsimonious model.
evidence: This describes the statistical modeling approach.

claim: Backwards exclusion of non-significant covariates at p>0.05 was used to arrive at a final parsimonious model.
source: We used univariable analyses (retaining significant covariates at p<0.1) and backwards exclusion of non-significant covariates (p>0.05) to arrive at a final parsimonious model.
evidence: This describes the statistical modeling approach.

claim: Community piped water coverage, age, toilet and sex were included in multivariable models regardless of their significance in the univariable analyses.
source: The exposure variable (community piped water coverage), age, toilet and sex were included in multivariable models regardless of their significance in the univariable analyses.
evidence: This describes the modeling strategy for key variables.

claim: Robust standard errors were obtained in models adjusted for the fixed effects of follow-up round to account for correlation among children who contributed data to both follow-up rounds.
source: To account for correlation among children who contributed data to both the 1st and 2nd follow-up rounds (pooled analysis), we obtained robust standard errors in models adjusted for the fixed effects of follow-up round and further conducted subgroup analyses on each follow-up round separately.
evidence: This describes the statistical approach to handling repeated measures.

claim: Gaussian kernel density estimations were used to describe the geographical heterogeneity of re-infection intensity.
source: Here, we used the Gaussian kernel density estimations to describe the geographical heterogeneity of re-infection intensity and identified the presence of significant geographical clusters of intense re-infection using the scan statistic implemented in SaTScan software.
evidence: This describes the spatial analysis methodology.

claim: The scan statistic implemented in SaTScan software was used to identify significant geographical clusters of intense re-infection.
source: Here, we used the Gaussian kernel density estimations to describe the geographical heterogeneity of re-infection intensity and identified the presence of significant geographical clusters of intense re-infection using the scan statistic implemented in SaTScan software.
evidence: This describes the cluster detection methodology.

claim: The normal probability model was used to examine geographical areas experiencing significantly higher intensity of re-infection than would be expected by chance.
source: Briefly, we examined for geographical areas experiencing significantly higher intensity of re-infection (mean log-egg count) than would be expected by chance using the normal probability model (Kulldorff et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the statistical model used for cluster detection, supported by citation.

claim: Every percentage point increase in piped water coverage was associated with 4.4% decline in intensity of re-infection among treated children.
source: Using a negative binomial regression fitted to egg count data, we found that every percentage point increase in piped water coverage was associated with 4.4% decline in intensity of re-infection (incidence rate ratio = 0.96, 95% CI: 0.93–0.98, p=0.004) among the treated children.
evidence: This is the main finding from the abstract, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The study provides compelling evidence in support of the scaleup of piped water as an effective control strategy against Schistosoma haematobium transmission.
source: We therefore provide further compelling evidence in support of the scaleup of piped water as an effective control strategy against Schistosoma haematobium transmission.
evidence: This is the authors' conclusion stated in the abstract.
